title: How to Catch Burnout Before It Catches Your Team
summary: Burnout starts as patterns in ordinary weeks: one person on every incident, late-night replies. How to spot it, make load visible and plan recovery as real work.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Nothing looks wrong on a Wednesday afternoon. Tickets are moving, standup was short, Monday's release went out fine. Scroll back through the project channel, though, and a few things stand out. One engineer has stopped asking questions in threads. Another now replies mostly after 10 p.m. And the last three incidents all landed on the same person, because they're the only one who understands the old deploy script.

None of that is a crisis, and each piece has a reasonable explanation. Put together, it's what burnout tends to look like a month or two before anyone says the word out loud. This post is about catching it in that window: what burnout actually is, which signals are worth noticing, and the team habits that take pressure off before someone runs out.

Burnout is a work problem first

The World Health Organization describes burnout as "a syndrome conceptualized as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed." It names three dimensions: exhaustion, growing mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. WHO files it as an occupational phenomenon and is explicit that it isn't classified as a medical condition (WHO, 2019).

The word doing the work in that definition is workplace. Christina Maslach, the social psychologist who wrote The Burnout Challenge with Michael Leiter, describes six areas where a mismatch between a person and their job raises the risk: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Her take is refreshingly direct: "It's certainly not just the person who has to make the changes" (CNBC interview with Maslach).

Gallup got to a similar list from the employee side. In a 2018 report on a study of nearly 7,500 full-time employees, the top five causes were unfair treatment at work, an unmanageable workload, lack of role clarity, lack of communication and support from managers, and unreasonable time pressure. 23% said they felt burned out at work very often or always, and another 44% said sometimes (Gallup).

Notice what neither list includes: "not resilient enough" or "should try yoga." That's why "take a few days off" rarely fixes anything by itself. Rest helps. But if Monday brings back the same load, the same one person who knows the module and the same deadline nobody re-estimated, the tank empties again.

The early signals look like ordinary days

One late reply means nothing. People have kids, time zones and bad weeks. What you're looking for is a pattern that holds for a few weeks, and WHO's three dimensions make a decent map:

  • Exhaustion: work keeps showing up late at night, someone whose estimates used to be spot on keeps slipping, small tasks eat a whole day.
  • Distance: someone stops asking questions, stops pushing back on scope, says "sure" to everything, or their jokes in standup grow a sharper edge.
  • Reduced efficacy: "I feel like I'm not getting anything done," from a person whose output hasn't actually dropped. Or they've stopped learning anything new, because every free hour goes to catching up.

Then zoom out from the person to the team. Who always handles the incidents? Who's the only one who can explain the legacy module? Whose name is on four projects at once? Who can't take a week off without the release getting shaky? If the same name keeps coming up, the team is borrowing energy from one person and calling it velocity.

Signals, not a diagnosis

None of this lets you diagnose anyone, and you shouldn't try. These are reasons to check in with a person and to look hard at how the work is split.

Make load something you can talk about

The easiest place to catch burnout early is a short, regular conversation about load, held before anyone has to admit they're struggling. Fifteen minutes in your weekly sync is plenty. Questions that work:

  • What's heavier than it looks on the board?
  • What's waiting on exactly one person right now?
  • What could slip a week without real damage?
  • Which deadline did we agree to before we knew how hard it was?
  • What one decision would take pressure off everyone?

These move the conversation from "how much can you take?" to "how is the work shaped?". Nobody has to prove they're tired. The team looks at the work together and rebalances it while that's still easy.

Invisible work deserves its own line. Answering support questions, onboarding the new hire, being the person everyone DMs when the build breaks: none of it becomes a ticket, and all of it costs energy. Put it on the board anyway, even with a rough estimate. It's also where Maslach's "reward" area shows up in real life, because work nobody can see is work nobody thanks you for.

Plan recovery the way you plan delivery

After an incident, a big launch or a long stretch of fuzzy requirements, the tempting move is to fill the calendar with the next urgent thing. Teams that run on-call for a living treat that as a design flaw. Google's SRE book caps on-call at 25% of an engineer's time, aims for at least 50% on engineering work, and sets a ceiling of two incidents per 12-hour shift, because handling one incident, follow-up included, takes about six hours on average. On-call is paid back with time off in lieu or cash, capped at a share of salary, which also keeps any one person from piling up shifts (Being On-Call).

When a team runs over those limits, the book's answer is to change the system: fix noisy alerts, lend the team an experienced engineer for a while, and in extreme cases hand the pager back to the developers until the service is sustainable. You don't need Google's scale to borrow the idea. Write down what a normal on-call week looks like, notice when you're over it, and schedule recovery as real work: a lighter sprint, the refactor that stops the next 2 a.m. page, a day off nobody has to ask for.

Spreading ownership is the kind of recovery that keeps paying off. Document the fragile deploy script. Pair a second person on the next incident. Rotate who answers questions about the legacy module. Each of these feels slower this week and saves you a much worse week later.

Let the truth arrive early

Burnout grows fastest where people feel they have to look fine. A healthy team lets someone say "this is more than we can carry right now" without sounding weak, "I need help with this old module" without sounding junior, and "this deadline needs a trade-off" without getting labeled negative. When the team goes silent instead, the silence is a signal of its own (more on that in When Silence in a Team Becomes a Signal).

Watch what your team celebrates, too. If every good story is about who stayed until 2 a.m. or who saved the release on their own, you're teaching people to hide the cost. Thank the person who saved the release, and mean it. Then ask the follow-up: what do we change so nobody has to save it alone next time?

None of this means removing pressure. Software comes with incidents, launches and customers who needed it yesterday. A team can go hard for a sprint and come out fine when it has a clear reason, a say in the plan and real recovery afterwards. What wears people down is running at that pace as the default.

Try this week

  • Add a 15-minute load check to your weekly sync and ask, "What's waiting on exactly one person?"
  • List your team's invisible work (support, onboarding, build questions) and put it on the board.
  • Pick one thing only one person knows and pair someone else on it.
  • After your next incident or launch, block recovery time before the next sprint fills up.
  • Next time you thank someone for a heroic save, add what you'll change so it isn't needed again.
